newsitem.title: TUNISIA: Tunisia completes 1996 borrowing, more next year.
newsitem.headline: Tunisia completes 1996 borrowing, more next year.

text.p: Tunisia has completed its foreign borrowings for this year but will certainly return to the international market next year, possibly in the U.S., a Central Bank official said on Wednesday.

"We have completed covering the budget's needs for this year. We will certainly go back to the bond market next year. We started with the Japanese samurai, then we got to the Eurobond, and who knows, maybe the next will be the U.S. market," he said.
Tunisia's three issues this year on international capital markets have established the North African country as a good risk, bankers said.
Central Bank officials said the three issues were concluded on satisfactory terms, both for price and maturity, and that Tunisia was now better known on the markets.
"The risk of Tunisia is now a good risk, particularly as the issues were for longer terms. Tunisia's name is now well known on the bond market," one Central Bank official said.

Tunisia this week signed for a $150 million syndicated bank loan for a seven-year term with a five-year grace period, priced at 50 basis points above Libor for the first five years and 60 basis points above Libor for the final two years.
It was Tunisia's second syndicated loan this year. In January, it refinanced in London a $200 million syndicated loan, with a five-year transaction priced at 70 basis points over LIBOR.
Last week, Tunisia's Central Bank said that 15 billion yen worth of 4.95 percent 15-year Samurai bonds were fully subscribed by Japanese institutional investors in less than a week.

"Getting less than five percent interest rate in Tokyo for such long period of 15 years is very satisfactory for us. As far as I know, Tunisia is the only Arab country to get subscriptions for such a long term," an official at the Central Bank said.
The most recent loan was signed with a group of 24 banks by Finance Minister Nouri Zorgati on Monday in Paris.
"We went on the market for $100 million. We were offered $217.5 million, and we only tapped $150 million," a Central Bank official said.

"There is also a good distribution in banks who subscribed. Seven were French, three German which is exceptional, four Arab, five Japanese, two British, one Belgian, one from the United States, and one from Luxembourg," he added.
The official said that the total resources Tunisia tapped on the international capital markets as part of financings for the state's budget deficit has so far reached $500 million.
He said that this year's loans would not have an effect on the debt ratio. "These loans were planned and integrated in the debt forecasts," he said.
Tunisia's government debt expressed as a proportion of gross domestic product has stabilised around 53.5 percent since 1993, the Central Bank says. The forecast for 1996 was 52.1 percent.
Tunisia started looking at foreign debt markets because international development agencies found that it had reached a degree of development which made it non-eligible for concessional loans.
Tunisia's last rating was BBB+ by the Japan Bond Research Institute
